# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–6 (Complete and Final – Updated 71)

## Setting and Time
- **Period**: Spring through late August of first year; Christmas/New Year period; nearly three weeks into new year (1832) just after Lords threw out Reform Bill; summer and autumn of first year; winter of first year; Vauxhall evening during spring of first year; spring of second year; summer of second year (current narrative point); narrative extends into future years; present day with Fred and Mary at Stone Court in white-haired placidity
- **Primary Locations**: Middlemarch, Lowick, Grange, Freshitt, Mirecombe, Salwick, Quenwick, Fenmere, Bryngate, Chalky Flats, Gulton, Highbury, Cheltenham, Tipton, Yoddrell's farm, Frick, Miremere, Riverston, Quallingham, Halsell Wood, Loamford, Brassing, Stone Court, Coldcombe, St. Peter's Place, Lowick Gate, Shrubs, Dunholt, Yorkshire, Staveton, Bilkley, Harrowgate, Melspring, Wilhaven, Salford, Chiswick Mall, Hammersmith, Soho, Thames, England, Oxford, Chiswick Church, Buxton, Kensington turnpike, Russell Square, London, Southampton Row, Vauxhall, Exeter 'Change, India (Boggley Wollah, Ramgunge, Budgebudge, Calcutta, Dumdum), Forty Thieves theatre, King's 14th regiment post, Highbury Barn, Covent Garden Market, Doctor Swishtail's Seminary, Bedford tavern, Thames Street (City), Royal Gardens, Quenwick, Wilhaven, St. George's Hanover Square, Lambeth Palace, Cheltenham, Great Gaunt Street, Queen's Crawley (Hants), Mudbury, Gaunt Square, Mansion House, Oxford Street, Swallow Street, Cambridge, Leakington, Squashmore, Bethesda Chapel Liverpool, Naples, Paris, Eton, Pumpernickel, Strasburg, Crawley parish, **Yarlton, Quashimaboo (Aid Society location)**

## Main Characters

**Dorothea and Will Ladislaw (Married)**
- Engaged after Will's return; now married with infant son; established pattern of two yearly visits to Grange; Dorothea's life mixed result of young, noble impulse; finely touched spirit with fine issues though not widely visible; full nature spent in channels with no great name; effect incalculably diffusive

**Mary Garth and Fred Garth (Married)**
- Inhabit Stone Court; seen in white-haired placidity at open window; solid mutual happiness; Fred becomes distinguished county farmer; produces work on "Cultivation of Green Crops and the Economy of Cattle-Feeding" winning agricultural meeting congratulations; Fred gradually saved enough to become Stone Court owner; three boys only, youngest resembles grandfather

**Rebecca Sharp (Miss Becky)** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- **Age and Background**: Age nineteen; father was artist/drawing teacher at Miss Pinkerton's academy—clever, prone to debt and tavern, beat wife and daughter when drunk, died after third delirium tremens; mother was French opera-girl; claims descent from noble Entrechats family of Gascony; mother actually a Frenchwoman (CLAIM: Mr. Pitt Crawley believes her mother was a Montmorency); had dismal precocity of poverty
- **Appearance**: Small, slight, pale, sandy-haired with large, odd, attractive eyes; white slender fingers
- **Accomplishments**: Speaks French with purity and Parisian accent; skilled musician and linguist; clever artist; sings better than Amelia
- **Character**: Determined to make connected plans for future; never blushed since age eight when caught stealing jam; capable of calculated charm and intimacy; droll funny creature; shows great knowledge of the world in her observations; finds devotional practices ridiculous; observant of family patterns; becomes inducted into most family secrets
- **Joseph Sedley Romance Campaign**: Upon learning of Joseph Sedley's wealth, determined "If Mr. Joseph Sedley is rich and unmarried, why should I not marry him?"; invited by Amelia; won over entire household through charming behavior; left alone with Joseph in drawing-room; occupied knitting green silk purse; established great confidence and intimacy; Joseph began eloquent speech "O Miss Sharp, how--" but stopped when music ended; continued presenting nosegays; Rebecca refused his request to sing citing low spirits; asked him to help finish green silk purse; Joseph seated tete-a-tete with killing expression, hands bound in green silk web; Rebecca thought "I might go farther, and fare worse"
- **At Vauxhall**: Took Jos's arm; sat by him on open carriage box; everyone expected marriage announcement; lost themselves in solitary walk among couples; at Moscow panorama, rude fellow treading on foot caused her to fall into Joseph's arms; Joseph told favorite Indian stories again (sixth time); at supper during inebriation, Jos clasped her round waist shouting "Stop, my dearest diddle-diddle-darling"; Rebecca started but could not get away hand
- **After Vauxhall - Rejection and Departure from Sedley Household**: George Osborne pushed Jos back into seat; Jos never came; household turned against Rebecca; Blenkinsop reported Rebecca reading Mrs. Sedley's letters and accessing trinket boxes; Pinner suspected Rebecca had taken Amelia's white ribbing; entire household (except Amelia) agreed Rebecca should depart speedily; accepted Amelia's generous presents with proper hesitation; received purse from Mr. Sedley; kissing his hand, asked to consider him kind protector; behavior affecting—Mr. Sedley blessed her, invited her to always come when in town
- **Journey to Queen's Crawley**: Immediately upon departure counted guineas and began planning; carriage passed through Gaunt Square into Great Gaunt Street, stopped at tall gloomy house with hatchment over middle drawing-room window; departed London by coach early morning with bandboxes; awakened at daybreak by charwoman; placed initially inside coach but at Leakington (where rain began heavily), forced to go outside as Sir Pitt is proprietor of coach and passenger wanted inside place; rode outside in rain for greater part of way; young gentleman from Cambridge College sheltered her kindly in one of his several great coats; young Cantab (called Master Jack) and guard both knew Sir Pitt well, laughed at him, called him "old screw" (stingy, avaricious); Master Jack promised to "flog 'em on to Squashmore" in revenge for Sir Pitt's slow driving with his horses; carriage and four splendid horses with armorial bearings awaited at Mudbury, four miles from Queen's Crawley; made entrance to baronet's park in state; fine avenue of mile long leading to house; woman at lodge-gate (over pillars which are serpent and dove, supporters of Crawley arms) made curtsies as she flung open old iron carved doors
- **First Evening at Queen's Crawley**: Interrupted by Sir Pitt in night-cap and dressing-gown who seized her candle, said "No candles after eleven o'clock, Miss Becky"; called her "pretty little hussy"; threatened to come for candle every night unless she's in bed at eleven; Sir Pitt and Mr. Horrocks the butler left laughing; two immense bloodhounds let loose at night, yelling and howling at moon; Sir Pitt calls dog "Gorer" (killed a man, master of bull); calls mother dog "Aroarer" (too old to bite, formerly called Flora)
- **First Dinner at Queen's Crawley**: Half hour after arrival, great dinner-bell rung; came down with two pupils (very thin insignificant little chits of ten and eight years old, named Rose and Violet); wore Amelia's dear muslin gown; to be treated as one of family except on company days when young ladies and she dine upstairs; assembled in little drawing-room where Lady Crawley sits; at dinner, Mr. Crawley haughtily corrected the name of a dish being served; Rebecca served soup on silver soup plates with mouton aux navets; ale and water brought in wine-glasses for young ladies; after dinner, jug of hot water placed before Sir Pitt with case-bottle containing rum; Rebecca and pupils served three little glasses of wine; Lady Crawley had bumper; retired to drawing-room where Lady Crawley took enormous interminable piece of knitting; young ladies played cribbage with dirty pack of cards; one candle lit in magnificent old silver candlestick; Rebecca offered choice between volume of sermons or pamphlet on corn-laws
- **Evening Activities and Duties**: Mr. Crawley had young ladies resume yesterday's discourse, each read page of long dismal sermon delivered at Bethesda Chapel, Liverpool, on behalf of mission for Chickasaw Indians; Rebecca now engaged as governess to Rose and Violet with established daily routines at Queen's Crawley
- **Saturday Morning**: At five, heard shrieking of little black pig; Rose and Violet showed Rebecca pig yesterday; also introduced to stables, kennel, gardener picking fruit for market; girls begged for hot-house grapes but gardener said Sir Pitt numbered every grape and giving any away would cost his place; girls caught colt in paddock and asked Rebecca to ride; groom came with horrid oaths and drove them away
- **Governess Strategy at Queen's Crawley**: Recognizes Lady Crawley (Rosa) is indolent, void of character, not of least consequence in own house; finds it unnecessary to cultivate her good will—impossible to gain it; directs chief part of her attentions to rest of family; wisely treats Rosa with cool respect but focuses on others
- **Teaching Method with Pupils**: Does not pester young brains with too much learning; lets them educate themselves; trusts self-instruction most effective; uses extensive library at Queen's Crawley (works purchased by Secretary of Tape and Sealing Wax Office during Walpole Crawley's disgrace period); library contains considerable provision of French and English light literature from last century; imparts instruction to Miss Rose Crawley through reading and play
- **With Miss Rose Crawley**: Reads together many delightful French and English works—Dr. Smollett, Henry Fielding, Monsieur Crebillon the younger (admired by poet Gray), Monsieur de Voltaire; reads "Humphrey Clinker" (which she tells Mr. Crawley is merely "Smollett"); reads French plays while telling Mr. Crawley this is for acquiring French idiom in conversation; compliments Mr. Crawley on his French language proficiency
- **With Miss Violet Crawley**: Violet has rude and boisterous tastes; knows sequestered spots where hens lay eggs; climbs trees to rob nests; rides young colts, scours plains like Camilla; favorite of father and stablemen; darling and terror of cook; discovers jam-pot haunts and attacks them; engages in constant battles with Rose; Rebecca promises not to tell Lady Crawley or Mr. Crawley of peccadilloes if Violet will be good girl and love her governess
- **With Mr. Pitt Crawley**: Shows respectful obedience; consults him on passages of French she cannot understand (though her mother was Frenchwoman); accepts his aid in profane literature and his selection of serious books; shows interest in his speech at Quashimaboo-Aid Society; takes interest in his pamphlet on malt; affected to tears by his evening discourses; says "Oh, thank you, sir" with sighs and upward looks to heaven, occasionally earning handshake; Mr. Crawley believes "Blood is everything" and congratulates himself on how she understands his words when the common people are untouched; believes her awakened by his words; thinks himself too fine and delicate for them; believes her mother was a Montmorency
- **Current Status (Summer of Second Year)**: Established as governess at Queen's Crawley; calculating and managing family dynamics to her advantage; accounts of Mr. Pitt Crawley's employment are not caricatures

**Sir Pitt Crawley, Baronet** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- **Financial History**: Estate never recovered from heavy fine imposed upon Walpole Crawley (first baronet) for peculation in Tape and Sealing Wax Office; Walpole was jolly fellow, eager to seize and spend money (alieni appetens, sui profusus, as Mr. Pitt would say); in Walpole's day Queen's Crawley had cellars filled with burgundy, kennels with hounds, stables with gallant hunters; now such horses as Queen's Crawley possesses go to plough or run in Trafalgar Coach; Miss Sharp brought to Hall in team of these very horses on off-day
- **Dignity and Appearances**: Though a boor, Sir Pitt was stickler for his dignity while at home; seldom drove out but with four horses; though dined off boiled mutton, had always three footmen to serve it
- **Debt Avoidance and Parliamentary Advantage**: Owes his son Mr. Pitt Crawley a sum of money out of the jointure of his mother which he finds inconvenient to pay; has almost invincible repugnance to paying anybody; could only be brought by force to discharge his debts; Miss Sharp calculated that mere payment of his creditors cost the honourable Baronet several hundreds yearly; has savage pleasure in making poor wretches wait and shifting from court to court and from term to term the period of satisfaction; said "What's the good of being in Parliament if you must pay your debts?"; his position as senator not a little useful to him
- **Parliamentary Position**: High sheriff; rode in golden coach; great ministers and statesmen courted him; in Vanity Fair he had higher place than most brilliant genius or spotless virtue
- **Other Background and Character**: Named after great Commoner; son of Walpole Crawley, first Baronet, of Tape and Sealing-Wax Office in reign of George II; family tree includes John Churchill Crawley, Charles Stuart Barebones Crawley, Queen Elizabeth's Crawley (forked beard, armour); rotten borough at Queen's Crawley produces "good fifteen hundred a year"; family represented in Parliament constantly; old, stumpy, short, vulgar, very dirty man in old clothes and shabby old gaiters; smoking horrid pipe; shining bald head, leering red face, twinkling grey eyes, mouth perpetually on grin; when in full dress took gaiters off, showed little dumpy legs in black worsted stockings; speaks with country accent; incessantly discussing himself; swears a great deal; sometimes coarsest and vulgarest Hampshire accent; pronounces avenue as "EVENUE" and nothing as "NOTHINK"; does not disguise his qualities; proprietor of coach and horses; drives very slow; stingy, avaricious (called "old screw"); never gives money to anybody; characterization as old, stumpy, vulgar, dirty, in shabby gaiters, smokes horrid pipe, cooks his own horrid supper in saucepan; always tipsy every night; believed to sit with Horrocks, the butler after dinner; could not spell and did not care to read; had habits and cunning of boor; aim in life was pettifogging; never had taste, emotion, or enjoyment but what was sordid and foul; yet had rank, honours, and power; was dignitary of land and pillar of state

**Mr. Pitt Crawley (Eldest Son)** [MAJOR CHARACTER]
- **Financial Hold over Father**: Baronet owed him sum of money out of jointure of his mother which he did not find it convenient to pay; this monetary arrangement was one great cause why Mr. Pitt Crawley had such hold over affections of his father
- **Background**: Named after great Commoner/minister; son of Sir Pitt's first marriage to Griselda/Grizzel (sixth daughter of Mungo Binkie, Lord Binkie)
- **Appearance and Manner**: Pale, thin, ugly, silent; thin legs, no chest; hay-coloured whiskers and straw-coloured hair; in full dress, pompous as undertaker; very picture of sainted mother over mantelpiece—Griselda of noble house of Binkie
- **Character**: Very earnest; high-bred propriety and respectfulness; seldom spoke to his stepmother Rosa, but when he did it was with most powerful respect; never let her quit apartment without rising in stately manner to open door and making elegant bow at her egress; taught butler to say "My lady is served" and insisted on handing her ladyship in to dinner
- **School Experience**: At Eton called "Miss Crawley"; younger brother Rawdon used to lick him violently; though his parts were not brilliant, made up for lack of talent by meritorious industry; never known during eight years at school to be subject to punishment which generally thought none but cherub can escape
- **College and Career**: Career highly creditable; prepared himself for public life through patronage of grandfather Lord Binkie by studying ancient and modern orators with great assiduity and speaking unceasingly at debating societies; had fine flux of words; delivered his little voice with great pomposity and pleasure to himself; never advanced any sentiment or opinion not perfectly trite and stale, supported by Latin quotation; failed somehow despite mediocrity which ought to have insured success; did not even get prize poem, which all his friends said he was sure of; became Private Secretary to Lord Binkie; appointed Attache to Legation at Pumpernickel, which post he filled with perfect honour and brought home despatches consisting of Strasburg pie to Foreign Minister of the day
- **Diplomatic Service**: Remained ten years Attache (several years after lamented Lord Binkie's demise); finding advancement slow, gave up diplomatic service in disgust
- **Return to England and Political Activity**: Began to turn country gentleman; wrote pamphlet on Malt on returning to England (ambitious man, always liked to be before public); took strong part in Negro Emancipation question; became friend of Mr. Wilberforce's, whose politics he admired; had famous correspondence with Reverend Silas Hornblower on Ashantee Mission; gave speech at Quashimaboo-Aid Society; in London if not for Parliament session, at least in May for religious meetings; in country a magistrate and active visitor and speaker among those destitute of religious instruction; said to be paying addresses to Lady Jane Sheepshanks, Lord Southdown's third daughter; Lady Jane's sister Lady Emily wrote sweet tracts "The Sailor's True Binnacle" and "The Applewoman of Finchley Common"
- **Religious Activities at Queen's Crawley**: Subjected servants at Queen's Crawley to devotional exercises before mentioned (brought his father Sir Pitt to join); patronized Independent meeting-house in Crawley parish, much to indignation of uncle the Rector, consequent delight of Sir Pitt, who was induced to go himself once or twice; occasioned violent sermons at Crawley parish church directed point-blank at Baronet's old Gothic pew there; honest Sir Pitt, however, did not feel force of discourses as he always took his nap during sermon-time
- **Political Ambition and Estate**: Very earnest for good of nation and Christian world that old gentleman (Sir Pitt) should yield him up his place in Parliament; Sir Pitt constantly refused to do so; both too prudent to give up fifteen hundred a year brought in by second seat (at this period filled by Mr. Quadroon, with carte blanche on Slave question); family estate much embarrassed and income drawn from borough of great use to house of Queen's Crawley
- **Proud of French Language Skills**: As diplomatist, exceedingly proud of his own skill in speaking French language (for he was of the world still); not a little pleased with compliments paid him upon his proficiency; Rebecca compliments him constantly

**Other Minor Characters**
- **Mr. Horrocks** (Butler at Queen's Crawley): Serves at meals; Sir Pitt believed to sit with after dinner; laughed with Sir Pitt when he seized Rebecca's candle; taught to say "My lady is served" by Mr. Pitt Crawley
- **Mr. Hodson** (Hind from Mudbury): Sir Pitt's estate manager; discusses farming matters; jumped out of carriage at Sir Pitt's order to rush upon little boys gathering sticks; cracked whip on their shoulders at Sir Pitt's command; discussed tenants and farming with Sir Pitt
- **Miss Crawley** (Unmarried half-sister): Inherited her mother's large fortune; Sir Pitt proposed to borrow this money of her on mortgage but she declined and preferred security of funds; signified intention of leaving her inheritance between Sir Pitt's second son and family at Rectory; paid debts of Rawdon Crawley once or twice in his career at college and army; object of great respect when came to Queen's Crawley, had balance at banker's which would have made her beloved anywhere
- **Rawdon Crawley**: Sir Pitt's younger son from first marriage; at Eton used to lick his brother Pitt violently; at college and in army had debts paid by Miss Crawley
- **Mrs. Bute Crawley**: Rector's wife; refused to visit Rosa (Lady Crawley), saying she would never give pas to tradesman's daughter; uncle to Mr. Pitt Crawley
- **Lady Crawley (Rosa/Second Wife - Deceased)**
- **Walpole Crawley**: First baronet; impeached for peculation in Tape and Sealing Wax Office; received heavy fine from which estate never recovered
- **Lord Binkie**: Grandfather of Mr. Pitt Crawley; patron who introduced him to public life; now deceased (lamented Lord Binkie's demise)
- **Other Characters**: George Osborne, William Dobbin, Joseph Sedley, Miss Amelia Sedley, Lady Jane Sheepshanks, Lady Emily, Mr. Wilberforce, Reverend Silas Hornblower, Mr. Quadroon
- **Background Characters with No Clear Connection to Main Plot**: The wife of Cobin Corrett left Quenwick and settled in Yarlton; Cobin Corrett followed her to Yarlton within the month; Jotho laughed at a story nobody else found funny; Thiena argued with the carter over the price of a sack of oats; Eldette Corrett laughed at a story nobody else found funny

## Critical Facts and Status
- Narrator reflects on Vanity Fair as "a very vain, wicked, foolish place, full of all sorts of humbugs and falsenesses and pretensions"
- Narrator identifies Vanity Fair: Here was a man (Sir Pitt) who could not spell and did not care to read; had habits and cunning of a boor; aim was pettifogging; never had taste, emotion, or enjoyment but sordid and foul; yet had rank, honours, power; was dignitary of land and pillar of state; high sheriff in golden coach; great ministers and statesmen courted him; had higher place in Vanity Fair than most brilliant genius or spotless virtue
- Narrator warns of "harrowing villainy and complicated crime" to come in story; present chapter mild compared to future chapters
- Parliamentary seat at Queen's Crawley worth fifteen hundred a year; family estate much embarrassed; income from borough of great use to house
